title: Thank Goodness That's Over
relevance: The founding text of the tensed-attitude argument; the argument is one paragraph at the very end of a paper whose subject is N. L. Wilson's tenseless substance-language
limits: Full paper read (about six pages). The target is Wilson's substance-language, not eternalism by name; the paper does not mention relief as a datum about value, and does not mention presentism or the A-theory by name. Later claims that it argues for presentism or A-theory are from secondary readers
locators: pp. 12-14 (Wilson's bridge theory of the copula); p. 17 (the 'Thank goodness' passage, final paragraph)
assumptions: Ordinary tensed speech such as 'Thank goodness that's over' is understood without a date; the dated tenseless paraphrase and the token-reflexive paraphrase are not what the speaker is thanking goodness for
conclusion: A tensed copula is not analysable into a tenseless copula plus a date; dated propositions are 'medium sophisticated' and not the simplest empirical propositions
proof_status: Not a proof source; philosophical argument reconstructed
open_questions: Does the argument bear on tensed ontology, or only on the semantics of tensed speech? Prior's own paragraph is about the second

title: 'Thank Goodness That's Over' Revisited
relevance: The most compact statement of the Prior-Mellor-MacBeath exchange, and a third tenseless reply (tensed facts without tensed properties)
limits: Four-page note read in full from a scan hosted by Stafforini; this is the only source in the lane in which Mellor's and MacBeath's replies were read, and they are read as Garrett reports them. Mellor 1981/1985/1998 and MacBeath 1983 were not opened. Pagination of the first page not seen
version: The Philosophical Quarterly 38 (151), 1988, pp. 202-205 as paginated in the scan
assumptions: Tensed sentences have tenseless token-reflexive truth-conditions; 'Thank goodness' is a non-extensional context; Parfit's bias toward the future needs a rationale on either view of time
conclusion: Prior's puzzle for the tenseless view disappears once tensed facts are separated from tensed properties and non-extensionality is noted; but the rationality of the bias toward the future is then equally unexplained on the tensed view (a point made by Garrett)
proof_status: Not a proof source; philosophical argument reconstructed
dependencies: Mellor, Real Time (1981; Garrett cites 1985 printing p. 48)
open_questions: Is Garrett's 'tensed facts without tensed properties' stable, or does it concede what Prior wanted?

title: Tense and the Psychology of Relief
relevance: Modern close analysis of the relief in Prior's argument, and of why Mellor's first and second replies are inadequate; reports Mellor's later position from Real Time II
limits: Author preprint read from the start through section 3 and the first lines of section 4; the positive account of relief as planning-linked (section 4 onward) and the conclusion were not read, so they are described from the abstract only
version: Topoi, forthcoming at the time of the preprint; doi 10.1007/s11245-013-9226-3; Warwick author copy
locators: sections 1-3 (Prior's argument; date-analysis; token-reflexive analysis and 'spurious egocentricity'); abstract for section 4
assumptions: The 'Thank goodness' argument is a transcendental argument from psychology to metaphysics; Prior's modal, tense-primitive semantics is the target
conclusion: Existing replies (Prior's own, Mellor 1981, Mellor 1998 after MacBeath) do not give a satisfactory account of temporal relief; Hoerl's abstract says it is an emotion tied to sophisticated planning and says this bears on whether points in time are fundamental in the semantics of tense
proof_status: Not a proof source; philosophical argument reconstructed
open_questions: Section 4 onward not read: what exactly does the planning account imply for the tenseless side?

title: Thank Goodness That Argument is Over: Explaining the Temporal Value Asymmetry
relevance: The one paper that both rebuts Prior's argument and offers an explanation of the temporal value asymmetry, with the empirical psychology laid out
limits: Open-access PDF read through sections 1-6 (the long extract was read, not every footnote). Caruso, Gilbert and Wilson 2008 and Van Boven and Ashworth 2007 are known here only through this paper. The authors list Mellor's Real Time II as 1988 in their references and cite it as 1988 in the text; Hoerl cites it as 1998. This note uses 1998
locators: sec. 1 (the two asymmetries); sec. 2 (Prior and two replies); sec. 3 (causation meets evolution); sec. 4.1 (Caruso et al. experiments); sec. 5 (evolution); sec. 6 (implications)
assumptions: Causal asymmetry; evolution of affect; the affective asymmetry mediates the temporal value asymmetry (Caruso et al. 2008); the explanation can be stated with or without tensed structure
conclusion: Prior's argument is a non-starter unless it is read only as a reminder that the asymmetry needs explaining; the causal-evolutionary account explains it; either the account is stateable in detensed terms and is compatible with eternalism, or the dispute moves to whether the explanation needs tensed structure
proof_status: Not a proof source; philosophical argument reconstructed
dependencies: Caruso, Gilbert and Wilson 2008 (Psychological Science 19, 796-801; not opened)
open_questions: Do the explaining causal and knowledge asymmetries themselves need tense?
Normative status: the paper says explanation need not vindicate

title: Against Time Bias
relevance: The argument that future bias and near bias stand or fall together, and the strongest compact statement of the temporal-neutrality position
limits: Read sections I-III fully and the opening of the Dougherty discussion; the regret argument is described from the conclusion's summary of premises, and the error-theory section was not read. Journal page access was open at the time
locators: sec. I (definitions of near and future bias); sec. II (economic vs philosophical views; presentism and B-theory give no ground for the asymmetry); sec. III (Dougherty's pain pump); conclusion (regret argument premises 1-4)
assumptions: Rational planning norms; avoiding certain regret is permissible; compensation distinguishes temporal from agent neutrality
conclusion: Future bias, like near bias, is irrational; one cannot reject near bias and keep future bias
proof_status: Not a proof source; philosophical argument reconstructed
open_questions: Whether the scheduling and meager-returns cases bind future-biased agents who cannot self-bind

title: On Whether to Prefer Pain to Pass
relevance: The pain-pump argument that future bias combined with risk aversion makes an agent act to her own acknowledged disadvantage; shows future bias can matter practically
limits: Open-access page read in substantial excerpt (sections I, II, the pain-pump definition and the summary of options); the table and the treatment of options 1-3 were read only in part. Hare's summary of the argument on PEA Soup also read
locators: sec. I (Parfit's Operations case); sec. II (time-inconsistency); the four options after the pump; sec. D 'Is time-bias irrational?'
assumptions: Risk aversion is permissible; time bias is permissible; vulnerability to a pain pump is impermissible
conclusion: These cannot all be accepted; Dougherty tentatively embraces that time bias is irrational but lacks an error theory
proof_status: Not a proof source; philosophical argument reconstructed
open_questions: Which of the four exits is correct; Dougherty gives no decisive ground

title: Self-Bias, Time-Bias, and the Metaphysics of Self and Time
relevance: The clearest statement of how tensed and tenseless metaphysics each treat time bias; the source for the claim that grounding it needs a tensed picture, and for its limits
limits: Author copy read through sections 1-3 (about the first half of the paper: egocentric and temporal bias, the three obstacles, four-dimensionalism and its alternatives, and the start of egocentric presentism). The rest of section 3 and the remainder were not read
version: Journal of Philosophy CIV (7), July 2007; author copy
locators: sec. 2 (Time-Bias: Harmony 2; Grounding, Generalization, Irreducibly Egocentric Preferences problems); sec. 3 (time-bias and the metaphysics of time; four-dimensionalism); the analogy to egocentric presentism
assumptions: Considerations of the greater good concern maximal states of affairs; the monadic tenser has operators 'it was the case that' and 'it will be the case that'
conclusion: If four-dimensionalism is true the three problems for reconciling time bias with the greater good are insoluble; the monadic tenser can solve two of them by stipulation but not the grounding problem except on a shrinking-block picture
proof_status: Not a proof source; philosophical argument reconstructed
open_questions: Does any tensed metaphysics give a reason, not a stipulation, why past pain matters less?

title: Why Is Death Bad?
relevance: Primary statement that the asymmetry between prenatal and posthumous nonexistence is explained by the temporal asymmetry of attitudes to experienced goods
limits: Read as a long extract (statement of the Lucretian challenge, the Nagel reply and its failure, the future-bias reply, the 1915/1925 example). The first part of the paper and the notes were not read. Hosted on a faculty-hosted copy, not the publisher's
authors: Anthony L. Brueckner and John Martin Fischer
locators: the discussion of Lucretius and Epicurus; the section on asymmetry of attitudes to experienced goods; the 1985 example near the end
assumptions: Death's badness is deprivation; people are rationally indifferent to past experienced goods as such but care about future ones; a dispositional claim about attitudes, not a metaphysical one
conclusion: Death is bad in a way prenatal nonexistence is not, because it deprives of future goods we care about while the earlier blank deprives of past goods we do not
proof_status: Not a proof source; philosophical argument reconstructed
dependencies: Lucretius, De rerum natura III (not read)
open_questions: The argument treats the rationality of future bias as input and does not defend it
